assessmentSummary.identity: A linear deceleration drill in which the athlete builds velocity over approximately 10 yards, then uses planned braking steps to reduce momentum into a defined stop or exit.
currentCardFindings: The current card has no controlled movement patterns, body regions, equipment, environment, population, load, or fatigue data.
Current difficulty values omit supervision demand, failure consequence, impact, and work-capacity demand despite the high forces and technical demands of rapid braking.
Stable-stick and reacceleration exits should be explicit variants or delivery profiles because they have different quality gates.
assessmentSummary.programmingDecision: Use as output or movement-intelligence deceleration work after lower-speed braking competency. Control entry speed and stopping distance, require a clear deceleration zone and run-off, dose both lead limbs, and stop before braking mechanics or confidence deteriorate.

evidence.sourceTitle: Biomechanical and Neuromuscular Performance Requirements of Horizontal Deceleration
claims: Horizontal deceleration is the rapid reduction of horizontal momentum and is distinct from acceleration.
A build-up-to-breakdown card should define entry velocity, braking task, stopping or exit target, and distance available.

evidence.sourceTitle: The optimal training intervention for improving change of direction performance of adolescent team-sport athletes
claims: Change of direction contains deceleration, braking, directional action, and reacceleration sub-actions.
This card is primarily linear locomotion and deceleration/braking; a direction-change exit is an additional variant rather than assumed identity.

evidence.sourceTitle: Biomechanical and Neuromuscular Performance Requirements of Horizontal Deceleration
claims: Rapid deceleration requires lower-limb braking force and coordinated hip, knee, and ankle control.
Eccentric force absorption, trunk and pelvis control, and foot-ground interaction are relevant to braking performance.

evidence.sourceTitle: Biomechanical and Neuromuscular Performance Requirements of Horizontal Deceleration
claims: Horizontal deceleration has high impact peaks and loading rates, with the largest forces occurring early in stance.
Entry speed, body mass, stopping time, stopping distance, and limb strategy materially affect braking demand.

evidence.sourceTitle: Biomechanical and Neuromuscular Performance Requirements of Horizontal Deceleration
claims: Deceleration forces and loading rates can exceed those in initial maximal acceleration.
Difficulty cannot be represented by external load alone and should include impact, braking skill, supervision, and consequence of failure.

evidence.sourceTitle: Deceleration Training in Team Sports: Another Potential Vaccine for Sports-Related Injury?
claims: High-intensity decelerations create meaningful braking loads that require progressive exposure and robust tissue capacity.
The card should track high-impact contacts, eccentric lower-limb stress, preferred braking limb, technical fatigue sensitivity, and recovery.

evidence.sourceTitle: Biomechanical and Neuromuscular Performance Requirements of Horizontal Deceleration
claims: A deceleration task needs enough approach and stopping space, a predictable non-slip surface, and clear traffic separation.
Entry speed and stopping demand must be constrained for athlete competency, limb history, surface, footwear, and fatigue.

evidence.sourceTitle: Deceleration Training in Team Sports: Another Potential Vaccine for Sports-Related Injury?
claims: Deceleration exposure should be frequent enough to develop skill and tissue tolerance but progressed rather than introduced as uncontrolled high-intensity volume.
Dose should specify approach distance, intent or entry speed, stopping zone, repetitions per limb, total high-intensity braking contacts, and rest.

evidence.sourceTitle: Alternatives to common approaches for training change of direction performance: a scoping review
claims: Field-based coaching can use an early braking intent, lower body position, and a forceful but controlled transition.
The athlete should build speed to the prescribed level, brake before the target rather than at it, keep the braking base organized, then stick or exit as specified.

evidence.sourceTitle: Biomechanical and Neuromuscular Performance Requirements of Horizontal Deceleration
claims: High loading rates make loss of braking control a meaningful safety failure, not merely a slower repetition.
Stop criteria should include pain, limping, repeated loss of the stopping zone, uncontrolled trunk or knee collapse, slipping, collision risk, and inability to brake confidently.

evidence.sourceTitle: The optimal training intervention for improving change of direction performance of adolescent team-sport athletes
claims: Change-of-direction and braking training should be specific to approach velocity, angle, and athlete population.
Linear planned deceleration should precede more complex reactive or severe-angle direction changes when competency is limited.

evidence.sourceTitle: Youth Training and Long-Term Athletic Development
claims: Movement competency and developmentally appropriate progression should precede more demanding exposure.
Athlete instructions should define the stopping target, expected speed, lead-limb plan, and successful finish in observable language.

evidence.sourceTitle: Alternatives to common approaches for training change of direction performance: a scoping review
claims: External-focus cues can alter braking and direction-change kinematics during field training.
Coaches should observe entry speed, when braking begins, step organization, posture, limb preference, stopping-zone success, and the specified exit.

evidence.sourceTitle: Youth Training and Long-Term Athletic Development
claims: The task can be scaled through approach distance, entry speed, stopping-zone size, predictability, and exit complexity.
Lower-speed walk-in or jog-in braking is a valid competency regression and should not be mislabeled as a maximal output repetition.

evidence.sourceTitle: The optimal training intervention for improving change of direction performance of adolescent team-sport athletes
claims: Deceleration, braking, direction change, and reacceleration are separable components whose demands vary with velocity and angle.
Approach distance and stopping-zone size can be modifiers, while reactive cues or direction-change exits require explicit variants or distinct definitions.

alternateAssessments.name: 5-Yard Build-Up to Breakdown
alternateAssessments.rationale: Approach distance is a dosage modifier when the prescribed entry speed, braking task, and finish remain the same.

alternateAssessments.name: 10-Yard Build-Up to Stick
alternateAssessments.rationale: A stable controlled stop has a different terminal quality gate than an immediate exit but retains the same build-up and braking identity.

alternateAssessments.name: 10-Yard Build-Up, Breakdown, and Reaccelerate
alternateAssessments.rationale: Reacceleration adds a propulsive exit and changes dose and quality gates without removing the central planned braking task.

alternateAssessments.name: Reactive 10-Yard Build-Up to Breakdown
alternateAssessments.rationale: A late external cue adds perceptual and decision demand and should not be implied by the planned baseline card.

alternateAssessments.name: 10-Yard Sprint
alternateAssessments.rationale: Removing the braking target changes the primary stimulus from horizontal deceleration to acceleration output.
